title: Smudged Memos
pitch: A clerk at an invented Bureau of Misplaced Things receives sealed memos in cipher, each one an absurd grievance built from a hand-written grammar, with a spilled-tea mishap blotting some letters. The visitor works a bench of frequency charts, repeat finders, shift wheels and crib-dragging to crack it, without being told which cipher family it is. Then they can forge a memo of their own from the grammar, pick a cipher and a blot level, and send a link that opens as a postmarked envelope for whoever holds it.
whyNow: Timeless: a daily memo gives a reason to return and the forge-and-send path makes the page spread person to person; autumn paperwork humor needs no news hook.

research.summary: Real cryptanalysis supplies the depth: repeated ciphertext fragments of three or more letters hint at the key length of a polyalphabetic cipher (Kasiski; confirmed by Wikipedia, a programming book chapter, a textbook chapter and an online tool), and once the length is known each column falls to frequency analysis. That gives a legitimate toolkit that scales from a shift cipher to a short keyword cipher. Daily puzzles commonly share a result grid that hides the answer, a pattern seen in Wordle coverage. State in the URL fragment stays in the browser but is readable by anyone with the link, so the memo is a puzzle, not a secret. Index-of-coincidence values were not verified, so the page computes them itself. All memo text comes from a bundled grammar of invented, harmless office grievances; nothing is user-typed free text.

facts.claim: Repeated ciphertext fragments of length three or more, and the distances between them, are used (Kasiski examination) to estimate the key length of a Vigenere-style cipher.
Once the key length is known, the ciphertext splits into columns that are each a shifted-alphabet sample, solvable by frequency analysis.

Wordle-style daily puzzles share results as a coloured-square summary showing guess count and pattern, so the answer is not revealed to other players (as of 2026-10-12, from a community thread and a news piece).
Data stored in a URL fragment is not sent to the server but is readable by anyone who holds the link, so the sealed memo is a puzzle, not a secret (HTTP Watch and Elliptic).

design.coreLoop: Open the day's sealed memo, a screen of ciphered text with a few tea-blotted letters. Use the bench to gather evidence (letter frequencies, repeat spacing, a shift wheel, trial crib words slid along the text) and pencil letters in; each hint spends from a small ink budget. Cracking it reveals a short absurd memo and a postmark card; then the forge lets the player compose a new memo from the grammar and send it. Variety comes from the cipher family (shift, keyword substitution, short Vigenere) staying hidden until identified.
sophisticationHooks: A real cipher bench: frequency histogram against expected English, Kasiski-style repeat finder, draggable shift wheel, crib drag, all computed client-side on a bundled word list.
Blind identification: the cipher family is undisclosed, and the bench's evidence panels (flat histogram, repeat spacing) are how the player deduces it.

Forge and send: grammar-slot composer, cipher and blot choice, and a hash of grammar indices that reconstructs the exact sealed memo, shown to the recipient as a postmarked envelope with an opening animation.
Spoiler-safe wax-seal share card: stamp, ink used, and blot count only, never the plaintext or the cipher family, drawn on canvas and copyable as text.
design.scopeForOneDay: Shrunk for one morning. Build: grammar and a vocabulary of about 200 invented office-grievance words, three cipher implementations (shift, keyword substitution, short Vigenere with key length 2 to 4) with solvers used to prove each generated memo is solvable, bench tools (frequency histogram, repeat finder, shift wheel, crib drag), a seeded daily memo plus a short difficulty ramp of easy memos, forge composer, hash encode and decode of grammar indices, envelope and seal rendering, keyboard and touch input, light and dark, reduced motion, making-of panel. Cut: rail fence, sound, user-typed free text, accounts, streak leaderboards.
risks: Difficulty: cracking a Vigenere with a bench is hard for casual visitors; mitigated by a first memo that is a plain shift cipher, a visible ink budget of hints and a reveal button.
Overlaps in category and mechanic with other word-puzzle candidates today; the forge-and-send path and the instrument-like bench are the differentiators.
Index-of-coincidence figures from the Rutgers lecture were not verified; the page computes them from its own corpus and quotes no external values.
Short messages may be ambiguous to crack; each memo is checked at generation time for a unique solution reachable with the bench tools and a minimum length.

The link carries the memo as grammar indices only, so all text comes from the bundled grammar and no user-authored text can be injected; the page states that the envelope is readable by anyone with the link.
Grievance humor stays about invented objects and offices, never real organizations or people.

Unverified sources: the UCF lecture notes, planetcalc page, Randstad explainer, daily-games site, HackerNoon article and LiveCodes docs were not found again; the page cites only sources seen on 2026-10-12.

verification.notes: Kasiski, column frequency analysis, Wordle-style spoiler-free grids and fragment-URL readability were each found in several independent results; WebFetch was not used on these hosts. Scope trimmed to three cipher families and an easy-first ramp; the main risk is puzzle difficulty, not data.
